extracted.intended_audience: emerging and practicing creative writers (fiction, creative nonfiction, memoir, poetry, short_story authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using the 'show, don't tell' principle in creative writing: how to transmit experiences to readers via imagery, verbs, and detail, and how to balance showing with necessary summary. Includes exercises to build curiosity, craft, and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, Don't Tell — core definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than asserting something for the reader to accept, writing should transmit something for the reader to experience. Achieve this through a mix of vivid imagery, descriptive verbs, and immersive details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: instead of 'The monster was terrifying,' use 'The towering thing was constantly morphing, tumbling over itself as it drew toward her.' Emphasize transmitting experiences rather than delivering information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create 'doorways' for the reader (empower reader experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show, don't tell writing creates 'doorways'—ways in that let the reader live in and directly experience the world of the writing rather than being told facts about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow readers to bring their own imagination and interpretation; give them an experiential and interpretive job beyond just understanding or agreeing. Accept and embrace ambiguity as part of this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance showing and telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not show all the time; some pieces of information are better summarized. A healthy balance of both is key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-patterns of 'too much show' (over-descriptive passages that slow readers down) and 'too much tell' (flat summary that removes immediacy). Examples: 'Too much show' vs 'too much tell' and a 'good balance' example are provided. Use telling to compress and get to the richest moments to show.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prefer telling (summary) versus showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use telling (summary) for material that doesn't deserve deep reader engagement: minor characters, uneventful periods, scene transitions, memos/notes, and intentionally to build contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists specific situations: Describing certain minor characters; Glossing over periods of time that are uneventful or unimportant; Transitioning between scenes; Writing memos, notes, dialogue, or other declarative media; Intentionally building a contrast with more evocative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory detail and imagery (five senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe using the five senses and vivid, specific details (not just labels) to convey what a character or scene actually feels, smells, sounds, tastes, and looks like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include: describe a character using only the five senses; remember a unique experience and convey its uniqueness through sensory detail. Use similes and metaphors (e.g., 'his eyes are like primeval forests').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer specific actions and descriptive verbs over adjectival statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Show by depicting actions and concrete behaviors (verbs) rather than labeling states with adjectives or abstract assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: instead of 'The man was cold' use 'He shivered and pulled up his flannel scarf.' Exercise: write without adjectives/adverbs, using only nouns, verbs, and literary devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene versus summary: show in scenes, tell in summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve showing for scenes where readers should be immersed; use summarizing (telling) for overviews or less important material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that 'showing' will be found more frequently in scenes, while summaries serve to move the story along or bridge passages quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity as the selection principle for what to show
rubrics_metrics.description: Let writerly curiosity guide which details to focus on—what doorways into the story are most fertile and interesting to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in an art heist story you might show museum layout, brushstrokes, a shaky laugh, a moment of joy, or social cues signaling relationship cracks. Curiosity exercises (freewriting, POV rewrites, imagining new settings) are provided to practice noticing vivid detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft fundamentals and literary devices enable showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing relies on craft fundamentals: figurative language, mood, patterns, associations, and other literary devices to convey complex impressions without explicit explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seven craft exercises are given: use metaphor/simile; write without adjectives/adverbs; convey emotions atmospherically; find and practice unfamiliar literary devices; transcribe dialogue and add physical description; emulate an author's style; use poetic/prose forms and genre constraints to force craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence and trust in readers (avoid didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must trust readers to interpret ambiguous material and resist the impulse to 'tell' the reader what to feel or think; creative writing demands accepting ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: don't erase ambiguity to control reader experience. Be clear about whether your piece is didactic (teaching/arguing) or creative (inviting experience). Cultivate belief that the worlds you show are worth experiencing and that readers want to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercises and drills to build showing ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice with concrete exercises across curiosity, craft, and confidence to internalize showing techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curiosity exercises (6 listed) and craft exercises (7 listed) give step-by-step drills: five-minute freewriting, five-sense descriptions, POV rewrites, reading like a writer, writing without adjectives/adverbs, using unfamiliar literary devices, transcribing dialogue and expanding, emulating authors, and writing within forms/constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read like a writer and study exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively analyze books and authors unfamiliar to you to notice how they pull readers into perspective and show things that surprise or engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While reading, pay attention to what makes the subject interesting and how the writer creates doorways; emulate those techniques in your own work.
